description: A rule that was built, measured and withdrawn, kept as the shape it was withdrawn over. `Model.objects.get(pk=...)` is how the largest Python web framework fetches one row, and the record-selector vocabulary was JavaScript's alone -- find, findOne, findById, findUnique -- so Django's commonest lookup was invisible to every ownership judgement in the model, across five Django applications in the corpus. The receiver is decidable without a type checker, which the Python frontend does not have: Django spells its manager into the call, so `.objects.` says both that this is a table and which one, exactly as the store model already reads it, and its keyword arguments are column names rather than parameters so all of them are criteria. Matching `get` that way added 41 findings across the six Python repositories -- 18 behind management commands, which the engine already sets aside at operator trust, and 23 on the application surface. All 23 were adjudicated against source and none was true. Eight were saleor mutations that declare `Meta.permissions` and are staff-only, a declaration nothing here reads; three selected a record nobody owns -- a storefront channel by slug, a promo code by code; two were confirmAccount and setPassword, which look a user up by email and then verify a signed token, the identity-establishing family this model has already adjudicated at 0.00 precision; three were linkding queries carrying `owner=request.user` in the call itself; three selected by a primary key the database had just generated; and four were archivebox, whose API scopes nothing by user anywhere, its sibling list endpoint returning objects.all(). The finding the work was for -- saleor's checkoutCreateFromOrder, the one mutation in that file that declares no permissions -- did not appear either, because it reaches the lookup through `getattr(graphene_type, "get_node")` and a name-based call graph cannot follow that. So the rule could not reach the one true case and could not tell the twenty-three false ones apart from it. Six views, every one silent, each recording one reason. `bookmark_detail` is the positive the channel was for and the shape nothing distinguishes; `_bundle_for` states the ownership relation IN the query one frame below the handler, where actor identity -- seeded only from a property read on the entry point's own parameter -- cannot be seen, and fired; `share_bookmark` selects by a key the database made, and fired; `token_detail` states the same relation in the handler itself, where identity IS visible, and was correctly silent; `search` is why `filter` and `exclude` were never added beside `get`, since a caller choosing which rows come back is what a search IS; and `preferences` holds the three near-misses that must stay silent whatever else changes -- a dict the handler built, the process environment, and a cache -- because `get` is written 10050 times across the corpus's Python repositories and only 1675 of those are on a manager. The routes use `<str:>` rather than `<int:>` deliberately: an int converter is a constrained converter and never seeds a source at all, so Django's commonest detail route -- `<int:pk>` -- carries no caller data into any of this, which is a second reason the shape has less reach than its call count suggests.
